rappel_detail.anchor: Fixed webbing at the true summit, no bolts. What is actually there has changed: a 2018 party found a home-made spinning hanger backed up to a rock pinch, and the local rangers stripped and rebuilt the tat on the lower (west) summit stations that same season because the accumulated slings had become impossible to judge.
rappel_detail.station: Essentially underfoot once you top out — the flat ground at the true summit. Parties who finish the West Ridge on the lower west summit should not expect an anchor there; at least one party in 2018 found nothing on the west summit and had to continue east to the true summit to start the descent.
hazards: The start is awkward — you squeeze into a narrow chute to get weight onto the rope, which is the least pleasant transition on the descent
Abandoned stations sit further climber's left of the current line and are explicitly not recommended; do not follow old tat leftward
rappel_detail.pull: This is the station where ropes hang up. One party's rope jammed on the pull off the first rappel and had to be freed by hauling on it with a progress-capture pulley. Pull from as far out from the chute as the ledge allows.
rappel_detail.notes: Noticeably shorter than the four rappels below it; the rest of the line runs close to a full 30 m.

rappel_detail.anchor: Webbing around a chockstone jammed between the main wall and a protruding flake. Relocated by the climbing rangers in 2018 — it is no longer on the big ledge that older beta describes.
rappel_detail.station: Not visible from the summit. Rappel roughly 25 m and look climber's left. Relative to the old ledge station it sits about 30 ft (9 m) climber's left and about 50 ft (15 m) further down the slope, so parties navigating from a pre-2018 description will rappel straight past where they expect it.
hazards: Cramped stance — the relocated station is on a pillar-like perch that is hard to stand at comfortably with two people
Missing it means either climbing back up or committing to unknown ground below
rappel_detail.notes: Every station on this line is tat, not fixed hardware; carry cord and be willing to replace rather than add to it.

rappel_detail.anchor: Fixed webbing (tat). No bolts anywhere on this descent.
rappel_detail.station: The one easy station on the line — from station 2 it is in plain sight directly below you.

rappel_detail.anchor: Fixed webbing, also relocated in 2018.
rappel_detail.station: Hidden, and the station people miss. From station 3 you must trend climber's left rather than straight down; it is tucked into a small alcove left of station 3, sitting just above the gully where the ground eases off to 3rd and 4th class.
hazards: The station sits directly beneath a large volume of loose rock, and getting down from it without knocking anything off is genuinely difficult — keep the rest of the party out from underneath and expect to be hit by what you dislodge yourself
The gully below is broken and full of snag features
rappel_detail.pull: Reported as having a great many places for the rope to jam. Flick the strands clear of the alcove and the gully edges before the last climber pulls, and think about which side you pull from.
rappel_detail.notes: After this rappel you can leave the ropes packed and downclimb 3rd class ground climber's right to reach the climbers' trail back to the base of the West Ridge — that scrambling is loose.

rappel_detail.anchor: Fixed webbing.
rappel_detail.station: Optional. Two further stations sit climber's right of the gully below station 4 and drop straight onto the climbers' path, rejoining the older rappel line.
hazards: Skipping these in favour of the downclimb puts you on loose 3rd class ground with a pack and a rope on your back
rappel_detail.notes: Taking the last station or two buys cleaner ground at the cost of more rope work; both finishes land on the same trail, which leads west back to Prusik Pass and the start of the West Ridge.

wa_prusik_peak_west_ridge.rappel_count_note: Five single-rope rappels from the true summit down the north face to the climbers' trail is the common count, and the line is laid out around one 60 m rope doubled — the first rappel is short and the remaining four are close to a full 30 m, i.e. rope-stretchers on a doubled 60. Reported counts of 3 and 4 are the same anchors under different choices, not different beta: with two ropes the descent has been done in three rappels (two double-length plus one single), and after station 4 many parties downclimb 3rd class ground climber's right rather than using the last one or two stations. A faster variation for confident parties is two rappels and then a hard traverse west to the West Ridge to downclimb. A party of three, or anyone wanting margin at the two stretchers, will be happier on a 70 m.
wa_prusik_peak_west_ridge._replaced: Overwrites 4 stored entries whose per-station lengths were unsourced.

wa_prusik_peak_south_face_burgner_stanle._remap: Requested as wa_prusik_peak_south_face, which does not exist in the routes table. Prusik's South Face is catalogued as wa_prusik_peak_south_face_burgner_stanley (there is also a near-duplicate row, wa_stanley_burgner, which shares this same descent and was not written here).

rappel_detail.anchor: Fixed webbing at the true summit; no bolts and very little fixed gear anywhere on this route or at the top. What is present has been rebuilt — the rangers stripped the accumulated slings off the lower-summit stations in 2018, and a party that season found a home-made spinning hanger backed to a rock pinch at the true summit.
rappel_detail.station: From where the last corner pitch tops out, walk east along the summit to find the start of the north-face line. This is the same descent used by every South Face route on the peak, so expect to queue behind other parties.
hazards: The start squeezes into a narrow chute and is awkward to commit to
Older, abandoned stations lie further climber's left and are not recommended
rappel_detail.pull: The first pull is the one that jams — a party on this line had to free a stuck rope with a progress-capture pulley after the first rappel, and another watched the party ahead repeatedly hang ropes up on this face.
rappel_detail.notes: The shortest of the sequence; the four below it are near-full-length on a doubled 60 m.

rappel_detail.anchor: Webbing around a chockstone wedged between the main wall and a protruding flake. Moved off the big ledge in 2018.
rappel_detail.station: Invisible from above — rappel roughly 25 m and look climber's left. It sits about 30 ft (9 m) climber's left of the old ledge station and about 50 ft (15 m) below it, so beta that sends you to a ledge will send you past it.
hazards: Awkward, exposed perch that is hard to share comfortably
Aged webbing on a natural chockstone — inspect it and back it up with your own material rather than adding another sling to the pile

rappel_detail.anchor: Fixed webbing (tat).
rappel_detail.station: In plain sight directly below station 2 — the only station on the descent you do not have to hunt for.

rappel_detail.anchor: Fixed webbing, relocated in 2018.
rappel_detail.station: Hidden. Trend climber's left off station 3 rather than straight down; it is in a small alcove left of station 3, immediately above the gully where the terrain relents to 3rd and 4th class.
hazards: Sits directly under a large amount of loose rock and is hard to leave without dislodging some of it onto whoever is below
Numerous rope-snagging features in the gully underneath
rappel_detail.pull: Reported as having many places for the rope to get stuck — clear the strands off the alcove lip and gully edges before the last pull.
rappel_detail.notes: You can stop rappelling here and downclimb 3rd class ground climber's right to the climbers' trail.

rappel_detail.anchor: Fixed webbing.
rappel_detail.station: Optional pair of stations climber's right of the gully below station 4, dropping straight onto the climbers' path and rejoining the old rappel line.
hazards: The alternative downclimb is loose
rappel_detail.notes: From the trail, traverse west around the base of the peak to return to the foot of the South Face. Figure about an hour summit-to-base if nobody is queued ahead of you.

wa_prusik_peak_south_face_burgner_stanle.rappel_count_note: Mountain Project's route description simply says to walk east from the summit and rappel the north face on slung stations with either one or two ropes, and that is the real variable. On a single 60 m doubled the standard is five rappels — a short first one and four near-30 m stretchers — down to the climbers' trail. On two ropes the same anchors go in about three. Trip reports quoting three or four are usually a two-rope descent, or a party that stopped after station 4 and downclimbed the 3rd class ground climber's right. This is a shared descent used by the West Ridge and several South Face routes, so allow for waiting.
wa_prusik_peak_south_face_burgner_stanle._replaced: Overwrites 4 stored entries whose per-station lengths were unsourced.

rappel_detail.anchor: A natural horn wrapped in webbing / in-situ slings on the east side of the summit block. No bolts. It is re-slung periodically because it is the standard anchor for every CBR route that tops out here, so what you find will be a mix of ages.
rappel_detail.station: From the top of the route, scramble across to the east side of the summit block; the slung horn is on that side and the rappel drops eastward. If you skip the balanced-rock boulder problem you can bypass the block entirely and never touch this anchor.
hazards: The upper pitches and the ground around the summit block are loose and lichen-covered — the reason parties are advised to stay roped rather than solo across to the anchor
Single natural anchor on a high-traffic descent: inspect the webbing and add or replace your own before loading it
rappel_detail.notes: Below the rappel it is a scree and talus scramble worked rightward — clockwise around the peak, roughly south then west — back into the basin and the packs at the base of the west face. Terrain under the horn is low-angle enough that some parties downclimb it instead of rappelling.

wa_colchuck_balanced_rock_west_face.rappel_count_note: One rappel, and that is the whole technical descent. Sources give its length as about 30 m from the slung horn; a shorter local description calls it a short 60 ft rappel from in-situ slings, which is the same anchor with a higher touchdown rather than a second station. A single 60 m rope doubled covers the 30 m and is what most parties carry — two ropes only buy a lower landing on ground that is already walkable, and the whole rappel can be skipped by bypassing the summit block.

rappel_detail.anchor: Fixed slings around a horn or flake at the top of the last pitch, on the ridge crest. There is no anchor on the summit itself — parties who go to the top build a gear belay there and traverse back to the crest station.
rappel_detail.station: Reached by reversing the exposed summit slab traverse from the summit block back to the top of the final pitch. It is on the crest, not on a face.
hazards: It is a ridge rappel rather than a face rappel: the start is awkward and the ropes want to run down either side of the crest
Loose rock is present throughout this descent and parties specifically credit helmets — keep the group off the fall line
rappel_detail.pull: If you intend to link this with the next rappel, the technique reported is to flick the rope over a horn so it hangs down the correct side; check the pull line before the last climber commits.

rappel_detail.anchor: Fixed slings around a horn/flake at the foot of the crux (5.4-5.6) pitch.
rappel_detail.station: At the base of the crux pitch, on the ascent line. It can be bypassed entirely: flicking the rope over a horn from station 1 lets a single 60 m rope doubled just reach the gully around the corner from the start of pitch 3, running rappels 1 and 2 as one roughly 30 m rappel.
hazards: If you take the linked option the rope only just reaches, and you arrive off-anchor — send the strongest scrambler first so they can get off rappel, reach the pitch-3 anchor and back up everyone behind
A rope that only just reaches is a rope that will not reach if the last person weights it lower or the ends are uneven; knot the ends

rappel_detail.anchor: Fixed slings around a horn or flake. At least one station on this descent was reported as a solid load-bearing horn with a useless backup beside it — a wad of slings looped around a handful of small loose rocks. Clip the horn; treat the wad as decoration.
rappel_detail.station: Below a long scrambling section that separates rappels 2 and 3, and it is one of the hard ones to find. Parties consistently report that the stations here are not obvious and recommend spotting and remembering them on the way up. This rappel also wanders off the ascent line.
hazards: Route-finding: this rappel does not follow the climbing line, so what you see on the way down is not what you climbed
Loose rock on and below the station
rappel_detail.notes: Some parties shorten their ascent pitches deliberately so that they belay at these stations and know exactly where they are on the way down.

rappel_detail.anchor: Sling anchor near the west notch below the technical climbing.
rappel_detail.station: The last and longest rappel, returning to the west notch. It wants two ropes joined, or a 60 m doubled if you can find a station that puts it in reach.
hazards: Easy to overshoot or drift onto the wrong side of the crest — one party ended up on the north side of the ridge and had to solo an exposed, loose pitch of 4th class to regain it
The gully below the notch is dirty and loose whether you rappel it or downclimb it
rappel_detail.pull: A long rappel on joined ropes over broken ridge terrain: set the knot deliberately and confirm the pull before the last climber leaves the station.
rappel_detail.notes: Some parties skip the final downclimb and instead rappel the loose gully straight from the notch. From the notch it is scree, talus and boot path back into the basin.

wa_sherpa_peak_west_ridge.rappel_count_note: Four stations is the standard description — two single-rope rappels off the top, a scrambling section, one more single, then a longer rappel to the west notch that wants two ropes joined (or a 60 m doubled where the station allows). With one 60 m rope the count drops to three by flicking the rope over a horn at the top and running rappels 1 and 2 together in about 30 m to the gully near the start of pitch 3. Reports of five come from parties who lost the line and added a rappel to get back on it, not from an extra anchor. This is not a clean reversal of the ascent: several stations sit off the climbing line and are hard to spot from above, and the standard advice is to note their positions while climbing.
wa_sherpa_peak_west_ridge._replaced: Overwrites 4 stored entries whose per-station lengths were unsourced.

wa_north_face_of_the_mole._remap: Requested as wa_the_mole_north_face, which does not exist. The route is catalogued as wa_north_face_of_the_mole under area wa_hook_creek_drainage (Icicle Creek, Leavenworth); the peak is also known as Edward Peak.

rappel_detail.anchor: A single bolt with added cord/tat. Every station on this descent is one bolt plus whatever webbing parties have left.
rappel_detail.station: From the flat, roomy top of the route the descent line drops the east side of the peak rather than reversing the north face — head east/down off the top to pick up the first station.
hazards: A single bolt is a single point of failure and this is a rarely-travelled route, so the bolt's age and the tat's condition are both unknown quantities — carry webbing and be ready to back it up or build your own
The east side is a gully system, so anything you dislodge goes to whoever is below

rappel_detail.anchor: Single bolt with supplementary tat.
rappel_detail.station: Continues the line down the east side toward the gully.
hazards: Same single-bolt exposure as station 1

rappel_detail.anchor: Single bolt with supplementary tat.
rappel_detail.station: The last rappel finishes beside the prominent chockstone chimney — the enormous chockstone at the head of the approach gully, described by one party as roughly the size of a step van, which is also the landmark where parties change into rock shoes about twenty feet above the start of the climbing.
hazards: Chockstone-choked gully terrain — a natural place for a rope to hang up on the pull
rappel_detail.pull: Landing among chockstones and chimney features means the last pull is the one to set up carefully; walk the strands clear of the blocks before pulling.
rappel_detail.notes: The whole rappel sequence can be avoided: the gully can be scrambled back down to the base instead.

wa_north_face_of_the_mole.rappel_count_note: Three rappels down the east side, ending at the prominent chockstone chimney, with every station a single bolt plus added tat. No source gives a per-rappel distance, so lengths are left unrecorded rather than inferred from rope length — do not assume 30 m simply because a 60 m rope is standard here. One older party reported reaching the notch above the start of the climb in a single rappel on a doubled 60 m rope after climbing a variation, which is a shorter, higher finish rather than a different count for this line. Parties who scramble the gully instead report no rappels at all.
wa_north_face_of_the_mole._replaced: Overwrites 3 stored entries whose per-station lengths were unsourced.

wa_argonaut_peak_northeast_couloir._remap: Requested as wa_argonaut_peak_northeast_face, which does not exist. Argonaut has no route named 'Northeast Face' in the routes table or in the literature; the northeast-aspect line is the Northeast Couloir (wa_argonaut_peak_northeast_couloir), which is what this beta describes. If the intent was the Northeast Buttress or the Northwest Arete, do not apply this — the Northwest Arete already carries its own four-station rappel_detail down a different line.

rappel_detail.anchor: Natural, and not guaranteed to be in place — the route description says you may need to rig the anchor yourself, and an older account describes rappelling from a slung tree on the southeast-facing ledge. Carry webbing and nuts for this descent.
rappel_detail.station: From the summit, descend back to the upper rock band; the single rappel from there drops onto the ledge on the southeast face.
hazards: No reliable fixed station — arriving expecting one and finding nothing is the failure mode here
You are committing off the summit onto a face on the opposite side of the peak from the couloir you climbed

rappel_detail.anchor: Natural / rigged; an older two-rope description used a stopper anchor part way up the southeast face.
rappel_detail.station: First of the rappels down the gully lying east of the top of the Northeast Couloir, entered from the southeast-face ledge.
hazards: Gully terrain, loose
Anchors may have to be built from nuts and left behind

rappel_detail.anchor: Natural / rigged.
rappel_detail.station: Continues down the same gully; the sequence ends on the snow slopes below, from which parties traverse toward the Colchuck-Dragontail notch or glissade the Colchuck Glacier.
hazards: Loose gully; the transition onto snow at the bottom may need axe and crampons depending on season
rappel_detail.notes: A third rappel in this gully is described as sometimes necessary, so treat the count as two or three here rather than fixed.

wa_argonaut_peak_northeast_couloir.rappel_count_note: The route's own description gives one rappel from the upper rock band to the southeast-face ledge, then two or three single-rope rappels down the gully east of the top of the couloir to the snow below — so three or four in total on a single rope, with anchors that may have to be rigged rather than found. An older account of the same descent used two ropes and fewer, longer rappels off a slung tree and a stopper anchor. A separate trip report on file describes two rappels down slabs north of the exit gully using two 30 m ropes plus a protected traverse across a wet ledge into the east gully; that is a different line down the same face rather than a contradiction of the count. Nothing here is a well-travelled fixed rappel route — bring webbing and gear you are willing to leave.
